issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and the opening of Section 3 claim that necessary second-order optimality conditions are proved. Section 3 contains only the first-order condition and a sufficient growth result (strictilocalopt, given without proof). No second-order necessary condition, for example nonnegativity of J'' on a critical cone, is stated or proved anywhere. The intro bullet itself claims only sufficient second-order conditions.

issues.title: Second-order necessary optimality conditions are claimed but never stated or proved

issues.failure_explanation: The implicit function theorem (thm:properties_C_to_S) gives uniqueness only inside the neighbourhood O(ȳ)×O(p̄). Navier–Stokes solutions far from ȳ may still exist, and the paper itself notes that multiple solutions can occur. So S(u) need not be a singleton. J(u) is defined as an infimum over all of S(u), so it may be attained on another branch. J then need not equal (1/2)||S(u)_1 - y_Ω||^2, need not be differentiable, and the formulas for J' and J'' are unsupported. The notions of local and strict local minimum, and the approximation argument, are tied to this J.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Work with the local reduced functional j(u)=1/2||S(u)_1-y_Ω||^2 on O(ū), or define local solutions as pairs (ū,ȳ) as in Casas–Mateos–Raymond. Restate local optimality, the growth condition and the convergence results for this functional.
issues.overall_effect: The following become unreliable: the C^2 regularity and derivative formulas of J, the first-order condition, the growth assumption and Taylor arguments, and the convergence and error analysis built on J.
issues.title: False global uniqueness of S(u) used to make the inf-defined J a C^2 functional
issues.why_classification: A standard reformulation of the local problem fixes the issue and keeps all computations. It still requires re-stating definitions and checking the existence and convergence arguments against the localized functional.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper asserts that the measure condition yields growth with constant max c_i. A larger c_i means a weaker measure condition, so it cannot produce a larger growth constant. The standard argument (split at |z_i|>ε and optimize ε) gives a constant of order (c_i(b_i-a_i))^{-1/γ}, decreasing in c_i. That argument also requires ε to stay in the range where the measure bound holds, which is unquantified here.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the constant by one of the form min_i (2c_i(b_i-a_i))^{-1/γ} times a factor, and quantify the ε-range or use boundedness of U_ad.
issues.overall_effect: The stated quantitative form of the implication, also used to motivate the appendix, is false as written. Only the existence of some positive constant survives.
issues.title: Wrong constant in the measure-condition-to-growth implication
issues.why_classification: The correction is a local, routine recomputation of a constant. The qualitative implication and all results are unaffected.

issues.failure_explanation: Interpolation plus inverse estimates give ||∇(y-ȳ_h)|| <= ||∇(y-I_hy)|| + h^{-1}||I_hy-ȳ_h||_{L^2}, which is O(h), not O(h^2). Indeed the gradient error is O(h) for y only in H^2/W^{2,r}. With a bang-bang (discontinuous) control, y is not in W^{3,6/5}, so O(h^2) gradient accuracy is unavailable. The correct bound ||∇(ẑ_h-z̄_h)|| ≲ h, inserted into the 3D inverse inequality with factor h^{-1/2}, yields only h^{1/2}. This gives ||ū-ū_h||_{L^1} ≲ h^{γ/2}, not (h|log h|)^γ.
